transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-10 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Arjun (Redwood SE), Sofia (CTO, Helios Labs), Liam (Lead ML Eng), Priya (Infra)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to triage an observed accuracy dip after moving a production backup model from FP16 -> GPTQ -> AWQ/INT8 variants. Primary goals: run a precision stability sweep, identify KV cache "hotspot" effects (prefix coalescing / stale KV), and design a controlled bisect that isolates which layers and which runtime paths introduce regressions. Also cover VPC/onprem perf differences and rollout mitigation patterns.

Topics covered:
- observed accuracy regressions after quantization (int8/gptq/awq)
- FP8 baseline vs int8 tradeoffs
- per-layer sensitivity and stochastic rounding
- KV cache warmup and hotspot / prefix-coalescing effects on generation quality
- batching and KV staleness interaction with throughput/latency targets
- VPC/on-prem kernel selection and operator differences
- rollout / fallback strategies (sticky canary, layer-fallback)

Action items (covered in metadata): see action_items field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: ok everybody, thanks for carving out time, I know this is crunch week; quick intros?
[00:08] Sofia: hey all, Sofia here, CTO at Helios Labs, will be brief on priorities — main issue is a ~3.5% drop in our rouge-like metric on summarization after we moved to a smaller footprint quant model, and it shows up intermittently in production.
[00:22] Liam: yeah hi, Liam, lead ml, we've tried gptq and awq variants, and int8, the perf wins are great but quality variance is worrying, sometimes it's fine, sometimes we get hallucinations mid-generation.
[00:36] Arjun: thanks, that variance is exactly what we want to chase down today — two main hypothesis buckets: quantization-layer sensitivity (some layers fragile) and runtime interaction (kv cache warmth + batching causing stale kv reads).
[00:49] Priya: priya, infra, we also want to understand the VPC-onprem differences; the same model behaves slightly different on our onprem rack vs Redwood's hosted test nodes.
[01:00] Maya: great, we'll split time: first per-layer sensitivity approach and experimental plan, then runtime KV/batching anomalies, then VPC/kernel differences and rollout mitigations. sound good?
[01:09] Sofia: yes.

[03:15] Arjun: ok starting with quantization — we ran a quick layerwise ablation where we kept FP16 on layers 0-3 and quantized the rest to int8, and saw the error reduce back to ~1.2%. That suggests the early transformer layers are highly sensitive for this model.
[03:35] Liam: that matches our smaller tests, interestingly the attention projection layers seemed particularly brittle. We also tried AWQ which preserves bias corrections and saw slightly better BLEU but sometimes weird tokenization artifacts — could be a tokenizer mismatch in the conversion.
[04:02] Arjun: couple of notes: AWQ often trades classification-like token probs for smoother perplexity; GPTQ gives smaller size but can introduce bias shifts with greedy decoding. Also FP8 experiments on our side show better numeric fidelity in the mid-layer activations but higher kernel latencies on some GPUs unless fused kernels are available.
[04:30] Priya: when you say kernel differences, you mean the math libs used? onprem we have ROCm + custom fused kernels for some ops, but hosted test was CUDA 12.2 and newer cuBLAS/cuDNN kernels.
[04:48] Arjun: exactly — kernel selection and custom fused attention vs reference attention can change numerics a bit. It's subtle but when you're on the edge, small drift compounds.

[06:10] Maya: can you sketch the sweep you'll run, Arjun?
[06:15] Arjun: plan: per-layer quant sweep across three methods: int8 symmetric, AWQ (asymmetric with per-channel scales), and fp8 e4m3-style. For each, we'll run stochastic rounding on/off, and two decoder modes: greedy and beam-3. We'll record token probabilities for the gold prompts and compute ngram diffs. We'll also capture KV cache traces — positions where cached kvs are read vs newly computed.
[06:46] Liam: capturing KV traces is new for us, how invasive is that?
[06:50] Arjun: lightweight instrumentation — we log a kv-hit/timestamp and whether the KV block was served from disk/cache vs warm in memory. There's a small perf penalty but it's acceptable for a bisect run.

[08:12] Sofia: when you mention KV hotspot or "hotspot" analysis, what pattern are you looking for?
[08:18] Arjun: two patterns: 1) prefix-coalescing where multiple similar prefixes cause the same KV entries to be repeatedly reused across requests which is good, but if a stale KV entry persists after a model variant swap, it can serve mismatched keys; 2) row-level hotspot where a small subset of token positions have large attention mass and quantization noise there skews outputs.
[08:44] Maya: and batch behavior? we've seen warmup differences when going from single-request to batch-8.
[08:50] Arjun: yes batching changes the cache residency and the kernel scheduling. With continuous batching, the runtime may reuse a single KV buffer and do in-place writes — if quantized kernels use different scale semantics you can get cross-request contamination unless buffers are zeroed or isolated.

[10:01] Liam: we did notice more regressions under bursty traffic patterns; quieter tails were fine.
[10:06] Priya: also our onprem has slightly older firmware and a different iommu config which impacts DMA ordering — could that affect memory aliasing for kv pages?
[10:15] Arjun: potentially. DMA ordering and page pinning differences can affect whether a reuse sees stale data for a few microseconds; normally that's masked, but with mixed precision and in-place quant writebacks it can matter. We'll log memory ops around KV warmup in the VPC run.

[12:33] Maya: ok let's talk mitigation ideas: sticky canary? layer-fallback?
[12:38] Arjun: we recommend a two-stage: first sticky-canary with KV isolation: route a small subset of traffic to quant variant but with a cold KV buffer (no warmup reuse) for the first N requests; then if stable, enable prefix coalesce. Second, layer-fallback where the runtime can dynamically use FP16 for specific high-sensitivity layers identified by the sweep. That avoids full FP fallback and keeps perf.
[13:05] Sofia: runtime switching per-layer is it expensive?
[13:09] Arjun: minimal at inference time — kernel dispatch includes precision arg; there's a tiny overhead on dispatch but it's far cheaper than rerunning in FP16 for the whole model. We already have a precision-mix path in the runtime.

[15:00] Liam: what about stochastic rounding? our ops teams worried about determinism in gen pipelines.
[15:05] Arjun: stochastic rounding reduces bias and often stabilizes outputs across quantized transforms, but yes it makes outputs nondeterministic unless you seed RNG. For eval, we run seeded stochastic rounding to understand distributional effects; in prod people either accept small nondeterminism or use deterministic rounding if reproducibility is required.

[17:20] Priya: on the VPC-onprem differences: any concrete steps we need to reproduce the variance?
[17:25] Arjun: please provision a test VPC with identical GPU types you run in prod, give us SSH access to a test node, and provide kernel/driver versions and any custom RDMA/firmware notes. We'll run an isolation test — same docker image, pinned driver versions, then log kernel selection and operator fusions.
[17:43] Priya: ok I'll spin up 2x A100 and provide creds by Thursday.

[20:12] Maya: runtime metrics to collect during bisect?
[20:16] Arjun: token-level latencies, kv-hit counters, per-layer activation norms, quant scale distributions, and embedding drift per step. We'll also collect generation diffs vs baseline and save full token streams for failed cases.

[23:05] Liam: we observed a case where after 80 tokens the model starts to hallucinate on a few prompts; could that be kv staleness accumulating?
[23:12] Arjun: yes long context can amplify tiny numerical shifts from quantized KV reads; also attention sparsity patterns can make a few kv rows extremely influential. We'll instrument to flag when attention mass concentrates unusually.

[27:40] Maya: any notes on AWQ vs GPTQ we should emphasize?
[27:44] Arjun: AWQ tends to be safer on generation tasks since it keeps per-channel scales and compensates for activation distribution skew; GPTQ can be more aggressive size-wise but sometimes shifts logits for rare tokens. For Helios' summarization workload AWQ appears promising but needs per-layer tuning.

[30:02] Sofia: are there off-the-shelf fallback heuristics? like if perplexity jumps X, switch layers to FP?
[30:08] Arjun: yes we can configure dynamic heuristics: if normalized logprob drops by >Y or ngram overlap below threshold for N samples, runtime triggers a layer-fallback or route to FP16 replica for that request ID. Those are pluggable policies in Redwood.

[33:20] Liam: curious about eval strategy — we'll provide 300 gold prompts; what do you want back?
[33:25] Arjun: return token-level divergence heatmap, per-prompt ngram diff, and per-layer sensitivity CSV with columns: layer, quant-method, stoch-round (on/off), avg-diff, worst-diff. Also mark where kv-hit ratio correlates with error.

[36:45] Priya: ops question — does the runtime zero KV buffers between requests or do you rely on refcounting?
[36:50] Arjun: by default we reuse buffers for perf, but there is an isolation flag to zero or reallocate for canaries. We recommend zeroing only for sticky-canary in early stages because the perf penalty is measurable.

[40:10] Maya: discussion of rollout plan: can we do canary -> sticky -> progressive prefix enable?
[40:16] Arjun: yes: 1) dry-run with small traffic and zeroed kv, 2) sticky canary where subset gets reused kv but with observability on token diffs, 3) enable prefix coalescing gradually and monitor drift metrics. If regression spike, immediate fallback to FP16 route for affected customers.

[43:55] Sofia: another ask — we need security/compliance note for onprem workloads, particularly around KMS integration during quantization artifact storage.
[44:01] Maya: we'll share our security comparables doc and details on cryptographic key handling for quantized model artifacts — that's in our next steps.

[47:30] Arjun: quick note on benchmarking: please run both single-request and sustained-burst (qps=200 for 5 minutes) to see perf/kv warmup interaction. We suspect regressions surface more under burst.
[47:50] Priya: will do.

[50:00] Liam: ok, final recap?
[50:05] Maya: Arjun runs layerwise sweep and uploads results by 17th; Liam prepares gold prompts by 13th; Priya provides VPC access by 12th; Maya shares security docs and rollout playbook by 11th. We'll schedule the 2-hour bisect next Wed once initial sweep is up.
[50:30] Sofia: thanks all — appreciate the pragmatic plan.
[50:38] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up in email with links to the data collection template and prebuilt eval harness.
[50:45] (call ends)

Notes on transcription artifacts: some proper nouns mis-transcribed (e.g., "kv cache" sometimes appears as "k v cache"), filler words and brief crosstalk retained.
